messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

Interesting problem! I am a little further North in Chile in Valparaiso and we have plenty of street dogs here too. Some stray, many belonging to owners with no gardens so they just put a dog house / box on the street. I have heard that when the council came round to 'take action' all the dogs disappear off the streets!

I think you are more along the right idea with strip transects using the street width as the width of the strip. Is my understanding correct that you are only interested in the dogs on the streets? So your study region basically comprises of all the streets in the town?

If this is the case then you have 2 options, fit a model to the data ignoring the non-street areas, and then make predeictions about the density of dogs on all the streets. This should allow you to identify areas with higher densities of street dogs than others. The disadvantage of this is that some streets will be close together in space but in reality the dogs may actually need to travel quite a distance to get from one street to another. So a better approach might be to create your study region so that it only consists of the streets in the town then you could use this region to take into account the 'real' distances between points. For example, a method like CReSS http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10618600.2012.762920#.VHx-M4dJlXk

I would say avoid garbage collection days. In my experience the dogs seems to form bigger pack on these days and travel further than they would normally. Sampling on garbage days I suspect would lead to lots of zero's and then a few very big counts, which is very bad for the modelling stage! On non-garbage days the dogs seem much more likely to stay local, I usually know which dogs I am likely to meet when I take a walk. I would say walking along the street, perhaps with a dog yourself, should draw out most dogs who can leave their properties.

What kinds of covariates were you plannng to put into the model? I guess you want to know if any of the techniques implemented are responsible for any changes, so including some measure of them. I also wonder if the level of provision for garbage collection factor. We have no communal bins locally, people just try to hang bags out of reach of the dogs, in comparison vina del mar seems to have a good system of communal bins.

Are you working on this with the Applied Ecology & Sustainability group at the Catholic University in Santiago? I hear they are looking at the stray dog population in Valdivia, although after a quick check they seem to be working in a more rural context.

Hope you find some of that useful,

Laura

Dr. L. Marshall

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews

On Friday, 28 November 2014, 12:50, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

> Adrian:
>
> The proposition is becoming a bit stretched.  You describe that you want a 'strip transect' to be the width of the street.  Then model-based tools to predict animal density where we did not sample (off streets).  The model would make predictions to non-street (i.e. centres of city blocks), which I submit would be not a good idea.
>
> Maybe it is simply late in the day and I have marked too many student papers today so my mood is not receptive to fresh ideas.  Perhaps other list members can be more supportive.
>
> On 28/11/2014 15:29, Adrian Schiavini wrote:

>
> Hi Eric.
>
> Thanks for the comment, you are true.
>
>
> I was thinking in modelling the counts of dogs along streets, using the street of each block as a "segment", to avoid issues related to dogs coming from crossing streets.
>
> Then I wonder if I can use "strip transect", taking the street width as the strip. At the end I should have a street traversed for let said 2 km, with something like 20 segments (depending on the length of the block), each segment with dog counts. How it looks?
>
>
> Also, it cames now to my mind that going behind garbage trucks may attract dogs from crossing streets as well as dogs from the traversed streets. Would this be a problem if I want to have an index to assess yearly changes only abundance?
>
>
>
>
>
>

> El viernes, 28 de noviembre de 2014 11:54:24 UTC-3, Eric Rexstad escribió:

> > Adrian:
> >
> > I won't speak to all of the issues you raise in the investigation of feral dogs in urban environments.  One think I will point out is the challenge of credibly dealing with the assumption that animals are distributed independently of the transects.
> >
> > The distribution of dogs in the vicinity (0-200m) perpendicular from the transect is not uniform.  Dogs know exactly where your transect is located and they are either attracted or repelled by the transect (as you note in discussion of garbage trucks).  You may see some dogs walking down the centre of the street, but many will be hugged against the walls of buildings that line the street; then occasionally you will be able to see hundred of metres down a crossing side street.
> >
> > As you know, distance sampling is based around fitting detection functions to sightings.  To fit those functions, you assume that the only thing causing the number of sightings to diminish with distance from the transect is caused by distance (not by parked cars or mounds of trash or garbage trucks).  Consequently the use of distance sampling methods in urban settings is challenged.
> >

> > If you can model the manner in which the dog gradient changes at small distances from the transect, then you might be able to produce both a model of the detection function and a model of the animal gradient.  See Marques et al. 2013 (http://link.springer.com/ article/10.1007%2Fs10260-012- 0223-2 <http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10260-012-0223-2>) for an example.  But as you can imagine the job is challenging.

> >
> >
> > On 28/11/2014 13:54, Adrian Schiavini wrote:
> > > Hi Everybody
> > >
> > >
> > > We are developing a framework for monitoring free roaming dog populations in the cities of Tierra del Fuego.
> > >
> > > The objective is to monitor the mid and long term success of the policies to reduce free roaming dogs in the streets of the cities, like neuter and responsible pet ownership.
> > >
> > > Cities are expanding in surface and adding new neigborhoods over the course of the years.
> > >
> > > For that reason, and to avoid restrictions of design-based surveys, we are considering the use of Density Surface Models, also to be able to explain changes in dog presence by covariates.
> > >
> > > Then, we should be able to tell the towns to follow a series of tracks (streets) that need to be surveyed over the years.
> > >
> > > Adding covariates, we should be able to develop a DSM to assess abundance based on these covariates.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Then, here comest the two questions:
> > >
> > > ONE:
> > > The issue that comes to my mind and I want to share with you hast to do with modelling all over the space of the city, when free roaming dogs are distributed only along the streets.
> > >
> > > The, the streets are like a mesh of something like 21m wide, separated by the about 800 blocks of around 90m side.
> > >
> > > Potential solutions I was thinkg were:
> > >
> > > 1. Model the data as if they were collected and build a prediction grid where blocks can´t hold dogs (as if they are "0") meanwhile streets has a value of "1".
> > >
> > > Then I wonder how much the smoothing all over the surface will affect the predicted results.
> > >
> > > 2. Model the data, but adding "dummy" transects located over some of the blocks, just to tell the model that inside the blocks   there are no dogs...
> > >
> > > However the modelling may be affected  by the spatial spread of these dummy transects.....
> > >
> > > 3. Use something like the soap film smoother but I can´t figure out how we can handle such amount of  blocks...
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > TWO:
> > >
> > > About detectability of dogs.
> > >
> > > When travelling along the streets we need to record  dogs that can walk freely at the sidewalks or at the streets.
> > >
> > > Streets has parked cars along the sidewalks, and many houses do not have fence, so dogs can sleep inside a parcel but leave the parcel boundarie as soon as they want to bark or whatever.
> > >
> > > This impose visibility issues that affect detectability.
> > >
> > > To reduce that I was thinking in make dogs more visible:
> > > 1. Survey the streets going behind garbage collectors, as these guys atract dogs either by their behavior (running along the streets) or leaving garbage behind ocasionally).
> > > 2. Broadcasting dog barks from the car meanwhile we go travelling.
> > >
> > > I know that this affect the results of a survey, but if we want to see dogs in the streets I understand that we need to make them out
> > >
> > >
> > > Any idea or previous experience in that is welcome. Many thanks
> > >

Sample sizes:

ETTI - Stratified by 2 samples, n1 = 66, n2 = 40
NOCA - Stratified by 2 samples, n1 = 81, n2 = 18

----------------------------

I’m using version 6.2 and have variable-width line transects. I came up with relatively low sample sizes (in DISTANCE standards) for each species.

1. When I try bootstrapping for Eastern Tufted Titmice (ETTI) I am

getting a bootstrap warning: convergence failure. Does this mean that

the bootstrapping variances for "D" are invalid?

2. In my Northern Cardinal (NOCA) analyses set, My attempts at

bootstrapping has always been met with the error: “Analysis Engine Terminated Unexpectedly”. Sometimes with an error signifying that there may be a problem with input or output files. I have tried different levels of resampling (e.g. samples vs

observations) and different numbers from 199 to 999 and I'm still

getting a crash. Is this because of low sample size or a program issue?

3. My "p", probability of detections are concernedly low for conspicuous

forest birds, my advisor says that they are typically at 0.8/0.9 but I'm

seeing 0.2/0.3. Does this mean the modeling seems to be invalid, or is

this just reflecting the reality of the sample? Note that there is an

interesting potential difference in observer "p" between treatments

because of the highway noise, but it doesn't show up as significantly

different for ETTI or NOCA sets in most analyses.

I really appreciate your time,

Best Regards,

Aaron

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am a new DSM module user. I’m constructing smoothing functions following the Dolphins sample project (which comes with Distance) and Miller et al 2013, appendix A. When modeling latitude and longitude as covariates, Miller applies a vibariate smoothing function, s(x, y), whereas in the dolphins project these covariates are set in two separate functions.

Is there any reason to decide between one choice or the other?

Thanks.

Alejandro

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Mcds distance sampling output and density estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

After an offlist discussion with Nathalie, I realised I misunderstood
her question and that the answer I gave below is not correct. If one
wants to obtain abundance estimates per *species* then one can use dht()
from mrds. You can use the "subset=" option to dht to select a subset of
the data to calculate the abundance estimates/densities.

[NB To do the subsetting need the Region.Label and Sample.Label columns
in the data, future versions of Distance for R will automatically do this.]

Having fitted your model (called my_model, say) one can now calculate
abundance estimates for a given species ("BW", say):

dht(my_model, my_region.table, my_sample.table, subset=species=="BW")

where the species column must exist in the data used to fit the model.

Hope this helps.

best,
--dave

On 13/11/2014 21:34, David Lawrence Miller wrote:
> Hi Nathalie and other listfolk,
>
> Regarding the model failing to fit, this may be down to the sheer number
> of covariates in the model. If you would like to send a minimal
> code/data example to me I can investigate further. It may be worth
> investigating goodness of fit tests/qq plots for these models (see
> ?ddf.gof)
>
> 1. How to perform a stratified analysis.
>
> First, it's probably easier to write your model in Distance rather than
> mrds (they end up as the same thing anyway, just Distance is a little
> easier to read (though I am biased)). You can write your model as:
>
> primates.cov2 <- ds(primates.covariate.fixed$data, key="hn",
>                  formula=~as.factor(forest) + species+size +
>                     mba.scaled + climber_perc + altitude.scaled,
>              truncation=90)
>
> You can then write you data in the flatfile format (see ?flatfile) and
> perform a "stratified analysis" as in
> http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html but here your
> "Region.Label"s will be the species. Then when you call
> summary(primates.cov2) you'll get the density/abundance estimates per
> strata (ie per species).
>
> This may or may not be biologically reasonable. (Others may want to
> chime in on this...)
>
>
> 2. Interpretation of covariate effects.
>
> This paper may be of use:
> http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/MarquesAuk2007.pdf pages
> 1234-1236.
>
> Plots illustrated in the paper of covariate levels are not implemented
> in mrds/Distance at the moment, though they are on my todo list.
>
>
> 3. Prediction outside of the sample from covariate values.
>
> This is possible via the flatfile format by including rows where
> distance is NA. However, if you think that environmental covariates (as
> opposed to those that affect detectability) affect distribution, you may
> want to consider density surface models (e.g.
> http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract),
> though this approach requires a relatively large amount of spatially
> explicit data.
>
>
> I hope this helps!
>
> best,
> --dave

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Sample size? Bootstrapping issues, wide variances for D and unrealistic "p"
messages.body_plain:
Aaron:

See comments below on your 3 issues:

On 01/12/2014 16:55, Aaron Grade wrote:
> Sample sizes:
>
> ETTI - Stratified by 2 samples, n1 = 66, n2 = 40
> NOCA - Stratified by 2 samples, n1 = 81, n2 = 18
>
> ----------------------------
>
> I’m using version 6.2 and have variable-width line transects. I came up with relatively low sample sizes (in DISTANCE standards) for each species.
>
>
>
> 1. When I try bootstrapping for Eastern Tufted Titmice (ETTI) I am
>
> getting a bootstrap warning: convergence failure. Does this mean that
>
> the bootstrapping variances for "D" are invalid?

I believe Distance does not use replicates in which there was a convergence failure in the variance estimates.  So the number of replicates will decrease when there are convergence failures.  You can check by looking at the Bootstrap Stats File (described on page 108 of the Users guide accompanying version 6.2).

>
>
> 2. In my Northern Cardinal (NOCA) analyses set, My attempts at
>
> bootstrapping has always been met with the error: “Analysis Engine Terminated Unexpectedly”. Sometimes with an error signifying that there may be a problem with input or output files. I have tried different levels of resampling (e.g. samples vs
>
> observations) and different numbers from 199 to 999 and I'm still
>
> getting a crash. Is this because of low sample size or a program issue?

Neither of your attempted fixes "resampling at the level of observations" or changing number of bootstrap resamples, are likely to solve the low sample size issue.  You note there are 18 cardinal sighting in your second stratum (not really sufficient to fit a detection function).  When resampling, it is almost certain that this number of sightings will be reduced (via resampling) such that there may be very low (or no) sighting in the stratum.  I would expect there to be a host of error messages that come from that situation.

>
>
> 3. My "p", probability of detections are concernedly low for conspicuous
>
> forest birds, my advisor says that they are typically at 0.8/0.9 but I'm
>
> seeing 0.2/0.3. Does this mean the modeling seems to be invalid, or is
>
> this just reflecting the reality of the sample? Note that there is an
>
> interesting potential difference in observer "p" between treatments
>
> because of the highway noise, but it doesn't show up as significantly
>
> different for ETTI or NOCA sets in most analyses.

The definitive answer to this question requires careful study of the data and the model results.  I don't know if your study used point or line transects; for the sake of argument, I'll assume lines.  My suspicion, given the values of estimated detection probability you report, is that you have fitted a spiked detection function that falls off very rapidly, leading to small values of p-hat.  Is the shape of your fitted detection function plausible?  Again in a hypothetical line transect, is it reasonable for your study that your detection function is near 1.0 on the transect line, but falls rapidly to ~0.3 at 5m (you miss 2 of 3 birds at 5m from the transect, which would be the case with a spiked detection function)?

If that situation is not plausible, then your data may be insufficient to support reasonable modelling.  Modelling and model selection is not a black-box; it requires judgement regarding plausible and implausible shapes for the detection function.

Hope that is helpful.

>
>
> I really appreciate your time,
>
>
>
> Best Regards,
>
>
>
> Aaron

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Smoothing functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alejandro & other listfolk,

I think this difference is purely down to historical reasons (there is a
considerable gap in time between the project being created and the
example written in the appendix). Sorry for the confusion.

Both separate smoothing of spatial covariates and bivariate smoothing
are valid approaches. Generally you might like to include two separate
covariates and see if one or both prove to be useful in the model (by
looking at the EDFs of these components and their p-values, inspecting
plots etc). One can also fit another model with the bivariate spatial
smoother instead of the two separate spatial smooths and compare model
fit based on AIC/REML/GCV and model checking plots (gam.check etc, as
detailed in the paper).

I have seen some data set where for example longitude does not play a
major role but latitude does and vice versa. As we say in the MEE paper,
these covariates are often proxies for covariates that we don't have
measurements (such as distance to a geographical feature like a mountain
range or sea shore), to they may not be particularly informative
biologically even if they appear to explain a lot.

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Smoothing functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alejandro & David,
Thanks for that explanation.  David, wouldn't you say that survey design/coverage probability is another factor to consider?  Several years ago, while analyzing data from a non-systematic (platform of opportunity) survey (http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol11/iss1/art1/) Sharon Hedley gave me a great example to illustrate this choice.  Imagine a really bad survey, with one N-S transect and one E-W transect.  If you modelled that as 2 separate univariate smooths, your rugplot would look like you had good coverage across latitude and longitude.  In fact, it's terrible spatial coverage.  A bivariate smooth would better reflect that gappy coverage -- in other words, it would let your model know that your smoothed interpolation was really extrapolation.  Is that a fair summary?  In British Columbia, we did a systematic line transect survey with even coverage probability, and the predicted density surfaces for frequently seen species were pretty similar between 2 univariate or 1 bivariate smooth (application described here: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2013.00479.x/abstract).  I'm going back about a decade, but I was also taught that one might rely on different diagnostics depending on whether you're primarily interested in distribution and abundance (e.g., semivariograms to check for unmodelled spatial autocorrelation).  The methods have evolved a lot since then.  I need to reread your MEE paper, David.

I'd also be interested in whether you'd give different advice depending on whether there is collinearity between an ecologically relevant variable and a spatial one.  For example, in our Antarctic minke whale survey (http://www.nature.com/srep/2014/140313/srep04170/full/srep04170.html), Natalie Kelly found that it was best not to include latitude as a covariate, because it was highly correlated with ice concentration.  We did use longitude.

Maybe you could tell us a bit more about your study & data, Alejandro?

All the best,
Rob

messages.subject_clean: inclusion of multi-year data for pre-/post-construction
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am analyzing raven density pre- and post-construction, but to do so, I need to estimate density using Program DISTANCE.  I am having trouble determining how to import the data for year.

Here is how sampling occurred:

point count surveys conducted 12 times per year at each location, 6 visits in the spring and 6 visits in the fall.
conducted pre-construction in 2011 and post-construction in 2014.

I haven't decided if season is important should be pooled for each year or if the density should be estimated separately.  My thought would be to treat each season/year separately (i.e., spring 2011, fall 2011, spring 2014, fall 2014) so that any differences in the ability to detect ravens between seasons is accounted for.

My main question is whether this data belongs in the "region" or "sample/point transect" layer?

Reading through the help topics on stratification and post-stratification for DISTANCE, it seems like the "region" is more for geographic data.  However, construction is altering the landscape, so I can envision a scenario where year is a function of "region" rather than the "sample".

A follow-up question would be how to make sure DISTANCE recognizes that there are multiple visits to the same point transect in each year?  I know how to do this for when there is only 1 year of data, but not when there are multiple visits and multiple years.

Thank you in advance,

Brian J. Bielfelt

messages.body_plain:
Brian:

My suggestion is that you take the simplest approach to the analysis, unless the simplest approach is flawed for some reason.

You are correct that "region" or stratum, often carries a geographical definition, but it is not necessary for that to be the case. Based upon the information you have provided, the simplest approach would be to enter your data with 4 strata that you identified (S11, F11, S14, F14) and estimate stratum-specific detection functions and density estimates.  I hope that with a study of ravens you do not have a shortage of sightings.

For each point transect in each stratum you associate a measure of effort; for points effort is measured in visits rather than in length of transect.  Hence you would enter "6" in the Survey Effort field for the points; if some points were not surveyed the full 6 times, you enter the number of times they were visited.  There are point count projects available as sample projects shipped with Distance; have a look at the "Songbird" or the "Amakihi" projects.

inform the modelling process and help avoid unrealistic models.

best,
--dave

messages.subject: analysing a very small sample
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,
I'm trying to estimate the density of a roe deer population in a small area (4900 ha), where it is assumed that the population is very small (a population crash was registered in 2003-2006). The area is almost all covered by Mediterranean maquis and forest.

We used line transect sampling and two observers covered 64 km of transects (the length of transects ranges from 0.4 to 1.6 km), 3 hours after sunrise and before sunset, using a lser range finder equipped with a compass to collect distance and angle data. The transects are located in a grid positioned randomly within the study area. The starting point is random within each grid cell. The orientation is random.

We carried out 4 replicates of the same set of transects (24 June - 25 September 2014; an average of 15 days to complete one survey) e we collected a total of 20 groups (3 in June-July, 3 in late July, 10 in August, 4 in September) and 22 roe deer. We surveyed in the same area also wild boars (tot groups collected: 939) and fallow deer (tot groups collected: 93).

To analyse data of the roe deer sampling, I used the MCDS analysis engine, I poststratified by replicate and I used a global detection function.
The longest perpendicular distance is 44.8 m. We miss observations in the interval 22-37 meters so I chose a truncation distance = g(x)=0.15
(10m), discarding 3 observations.

I estimated a global density as a mean of replicates, weighted by total effort in each replicate, and I used a nonparametric bootstrap to estimate the variance of the density.
As expected, several error messages appeared:
**Warning: There are less than 10 data points per estimated parameter. Results may not be reliable.**
**Bootstrap Warning: There are no cluster size observations selected. Cannot estimate expected cluster size.**
**Bootstrap Warning: Number of cluster size measurements =  1  This is not sufficient to estimate a mean and variance**
**Bootstrap Warning: Estimation routine failed to converge as could not calculate area under pdf in iteration 48. Using results from previous iteration.**

Despite the very small sample, is this the right way to tackle with the analysis of this data in order to get a density estimate anyway?

Any suggestion to improve the analysis of so few observations? (without changing survey technique)

Cheers,
Barbara

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] comparison of e.g. data set with two or more categories
messages.body_plain:
Nicolai:

The absence of sightings on a transect is not equivalent to "NA" the lack of sightings is itself information, so do not consider that as "missing data".  The transect was walked (or flown, ...) and nothing was sighted.  The amount of survey effort associated with the transect needs to be recorded as part of your survey protocol.

For valid inference, your control and two treatment areas should have replicate transects placed in them.  Hopefully there is sufficient replication such that you can produce density estimates (and measures of precision) for each of the 3 areas being investigated.  If so, then section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001) can provide guidance on making comparisons of density estimates.
